title: Team
text: The REPBIAS project has a first-class multidisciplinary academic team with researchers from leading universities around the world.

title: Team
text:
Principal Investigator
Marc Guinjoan is the Principal Investigator of the project. Guinjoan is an Associate Professor at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona and previously was a research fellow at the Institutions and Political Economy Research Group (IPErG, Universitat de Barcelona), headed by Carles Boix. One of the main fields of interest of the PI is the study of electoral institutions. His thesis dissertation dealt with this topic and was published in 2014 by Routledge. He has also several journal articles on electoral institutions published in Government and Opposition, Public Opinion Quarterly and Social Science Quarterly, among others.

title: Team
text:
Research Team
Carles Boix is a Distinguished Professor at the IPErG (UB) and Robert Garrett professor at Princeton University. As director of the IPErG, Boix was the team leader in the Beramendi et al. (2021) project and has in-depth knowledge and publication record on the field of electoral institutions. In particular, Boix has largely worked on the endogenous origins of institutions (Boix 1999; Abramson and Boix 2019; Boix and Stokes 2003), as well as on historical political economy (Boix 2010; Amat et al. 2020; Basu et al. 2019; Boix and Rosenbluth 2014). Boix’s publications have appeared in journals such as APSR (6 articles), AJPS (3), International Organization (2), CPS, the JoP, BJPS (2), World Politics (3); in addition, he has three books in Cambridge University Press and one book in Princeton University Press, among others.





Jordi Mas obtained his PhD in 2016 and his research interests include political economy, international politics, regionalism, and methodology in social sciences. His work has been published in the JCMS. As an expert in R Statistics, Mas guides and supervises the methodological parts of the REPBIAS project that require the usage of extensive quantitative data.

title: Team
text:
Working Team
Pablo Beramendi is full professor at Duke University. His work focuses on different aspects of the political economy of inequality and redistribution, paying particular attention to the territorial dimension of distributive conflicts. Beramendi has articles published in CPS (4), IO, JoP (2), BJPS, WP, EJPR, Annual Review of Political Science, the Review of International Organizations (RIO), and 2 books in Cambridge University Press.





Melissa Rogers is associate professor at the Claremont Graduate University. She is a specialist in comparative politics, political geography, political economy, Latin American politics, and comparative political institutions. Her work has been published in the JoP (2), Political Analysis (2), RIO and she has one book in Cambridge University Press.





Toni Rodon is Associate Professor at Universitat Pompeu Fabra. His research interests include electoral participation, political geography, comparative politics and historical political economy. Rodon has extensively worked with data on the Second Republic (Rodon 2020; Muñoz et al. 2017; Amat et al. 2020) and contributes to the project’s historical data work on electoral coordination and caciquismo. He has published in journals such as the APSR, JoP (2), BJPS, PSRM, Political Geography, JEPP and Socio-Economic Review.





Nikandros Ioannidis is a researcher at the Cyprus University of Technology, School of Communication and Media Studies. He joined the project through a collaboration on Voting Advice Applications (VAA), co-authoring “How Tailored Information Influences Election Dynamics” with the REPBIAS team.

title: Team
text:
PhD Student
Jaime Bordel is a PhD candidate (FPI fellow) at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, supervised by Marc Guinjoan. He is the author of the book “Salvini & Meloni. Hijos de la misma rabia” and holds a Master in Social Sciences (Instituto Carlos III-Juan March). His doctoral thesis — on electoral reforms in authoritarian regimes and citizens’ evaluations of electoral rules — comprises four papers, all developed within the REPBIAS project.

David Carbonell is a political scientist (Universitat de Barcelona) and a data analyst, working on the project’s simulation framework.

Xavier Roura is a Political Scientist (Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona) and holds a Master in Institutions and Political Economy (Universitat de Barcelona). He was a Research Assistant on the project between 2023 and 2024.

  Distorted Democracies
  Pablo Beramendi, Carles Boix, Marc Guinjoan, Melissa Rogers
  
    AggregateCross-countryContemporary
  
  To evaluate the extent of malapportionment, that is, the discrepancy between the relative allocation of seats and the relative allocation of votes across districts, we compile and examine a new, comprehensive dataset that includes population and allocation of seats by district and partisan ideology in over 20,000 districts and 1,100 different parties across 65 democracies during the period 1996-2020 in lower and upper chambers. In addition, we pool Spanish survey data (N=488,000) to examine directly how voters' preferences translate into representation as mediated by malapportionment. Our evidence shows that malapportionment is larger in upper than in lower chambers. Contrary to established views, we find that malapportionment is ideologically neutral in the vast majority of lower house elections, and where a detectable bias exists, it is as likely to favor the left as the right. Upper houses present a sharper asymmetry: a rightward bias predominates, and among cases of strong bias, it is exclusively rightward.



  Electoral institutions, malapportionment and the representation of ethnic minorities
  Marc Guinjoan, Jordi Mas, Xavier Roura
  Territory, Politics and Governance (forthcoming)
  
    AggregateCross-countryContemporary
  
  The representation of ethnic minorities in national legislatures varies widely: in some cases minorities are privileged through ethnic reserved seats or territorial concentration, while in others they remain systematically excluded. This paper addresses a gap in the literature by introducing a novel cross-national dataset covering more than 22,000 legislative districts in 84 countries (1996–2020) in lower-house elections, which for the first time identifies, at the district level, the presence of ethnic minorities excluded from executive power. Our empirical analyses show that countries with ethnic reserved seats for minorities tend to exhibit higher malapportionment, and that minority-concentrated districts are more often over-represented. We also find that over-representation is most pronounced in open autocracies and weak democracies, a pattern consistent with the strategic use of electoral rules.



  Unpacking Representation Bias: A Simulation Approach to Electoral Institutions
  Marc Guinjoan, David Carbonell, Melissa Rogers
  
    AggregateCross-countryContemporary
  
  This paper develops a simulation-based framework to decompose ideological representation bias — the gap between the ideological center of the electorate and that of the elected legislature — into the distinct institutional sources that produce it. We simulate large numbers of synthetic polities (100 districts, up to 10,000 runs per exercise) in which four institutional parameters — malapportionment, district magnitude, the seat-allocation formula, and the legal electoral threshold — are introduced exogenously and independently of each other, and validate the decomposition against real electoral data from Spain's 2019 European Parliament election. Results show that malapportionment bias is generally modest under random territorial imbalance but can become substantial when ideologically concentrated; that seat representation bias is consistently the dominant source of distortion; and that legal thresholds generate meaningful bias only well above common European practice. We accompany the paper with REPBIAS, an open-source Shiny application for research and classroom use.

  Historical Malapportionment and Elite Redistricting Strategies
  Marc Guinjoan, Carles Boix, Pablo Beramendi
  
    AggregateCross-countryHistorical
  
  Working paper — abstract not yet available. Traces the historical evolution of legislative apportionment across 14 countries over almost two centuries (1832–2022), covering more than 67,000 district-election observations, to examine how electoral districts were redrawn across successive reforms and what this reveals about elite redistricting strategies.



  Strategic Distortions: Electoral Reforms in Authoritarian Regimes
  Jaime Bordel
  
    AggregateCross-countryContemporary
  
  The literature on electoral reforms in authoritarian regimes has gained increasing relevance in recent years. However, two fundamental questions remain unresolved: when do autocrats reform electoral rules, and why do they adopt some types of reforms over others? This paper argues that electoral reforms are strategic responses to bottom-up pressures rather than signs of liberalization or regime strength, and that the salience of ethnic cleavages conditions the content of reform. Using an original dataset covering all electoral reforms in electoral autocracies from 1980 to 2023, the empirical evidence shows that authoritarian control problems increase the likelihood of reform, while ethnic fractionalization significantly raises the probability of adopting partisan-biased reforms.



  How Tailored Information Influences Election Dynamics
  Marc Guinjoan, Nikandros Ioannidis, Toni Rodon, Fernando Mendez, Costas Djoivas
  
    IndividualSpainContemporary
  
  Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) have become increasingly popular tools for delivering personalized political information to voters ahead of elections. Using an experimental design deployed in Spain during the 2023 national election (N=156,403) — the largest VAA experiment ever fielded — we identify the causal effect of party information provision on voters' likelihood of supporting a given party. Users exposed to personalized information reported significantly higher probabilities of voting for the party they already intended to support, and a lower vote intention for other parties within the same ideological bloc; the effect was strongest among undecided voters. Overall, the evidence suggests that VAAs may reinforce existing predispositions to vote for a preselected party, but we find no indication that they lead to vote switching.



  Beyond Partisanship: Territorial and Negative Self-Interest in Electoral System Evaluations
  Jaime Bordel
  
    IndividualSpainContemporary
  
  Research on how citizens evaluate electoral rules typically contrasts explanations based on normative principles with those centered on partisan self-interest. This paper develops a self-interest-based framework showing that self-interest can operate along multiple political cleavages beyond partisanship, incorporating territorial self-interest, and that negative information about how rules treat disliked actors can be especially mobilizing. A vignette survey experiment in Spain (n = 3,010) shows that partisan and territorial self-interest shape citizens' evaluations in uneven ways across ideological blocks: treatments signaling that partisan actors were disadvantaged reduced satisfaction among both left- and right-wing voters, while treatments activating territorial conflict produced larger shifts among right-wing respondents.



  Legacies of Caciquism on Electoral Coordination
  Jaime Bordel-Gil, Marc Guinjoan, Toni Rodon, Pau Vall-Prat
  
    AggregateSpainHistorical
  
  Early draft — abstract not yet available. Examines how exposure to caciquismo — clientelist electoral control — during the Spanish Restoration shaped electoral coordination decades later, during the Second Republic (1931–1936). Using a regression discontinuity design around historical district borders, the paper shows that municipalities more exposed to clientelist control display a higher share of wasted votes once competitive elections return, consistent with the erosion of the civic and partisan structures voters rely on to coordinate their choices.



  Conjoint electoral systems
  Jaime Bordel
  
    IndividualSpainContemporary
  
  Fieldwork scheduled for October 2026 — abstract not yet available. A conjoint survey experiment on electoral system preferences — the fourth and final paper of Jaime Bordel's doctoral thesis.

title: The Sources of Representation Bias
text:
REPBIAS · PID2021-128332NA-I00
    
    Why elected representatives rarely mirror the electorate that put them there — and how one overlooked institution, malapportionment, shapes who gets heard.
  
  ↓ scroll to explore

title: The Sources of Representation Bias
text:
What is representation bias?
Modern parliaments are rarely a mirror of the societies that elect them. The preferences of policy-makers — and the policies they enact — are seldom fully congruent with those of the citizens they represent. Political science has traditionally explained this representation bias through three lenses: who gets elected (elite selection), who turns out to vote (electoral participation), and the rules of the game (electoral institutions).
REPBIAS focuses on the third lens, and in particular on one institution that has received comparatively little attention despite its consequences: malapportionment — the mismatch between the share of seats and the share of votes (or population) allocated to each electoral district. When districts of very different sizes elect the same number of representatives, some votes simply count more than others.

title: The Sources of Representation Bias
text:
What the project does
The sources of representation bias: An historical political economy approach (REPBIAS) is led by Marc Guinjoan (Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona) as Principal Investigator, and funded by the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation (PID2021-128332NA-I00).
The project works at two levels. First, at the aggregate level: how much does malapportionment actually distort representation, compared with district magnitude, seat-allocation formulas, or legal thresholds? Where does it come from historically, and have elites used it to entrench their own power? What role does it play in protecting or excluding ethnic and national minorities? Second, once these aggregate distortions are mapped out, the project moves to the individual level: how do citizens perceive and evaluate the electoral rules that shape their representation, and does the information they receive actually change how they vote?

title: The Sources of Representation Bias
text:
Main findings


🗳️

District magnitude, not malapportionment, still rules
Across 65 democracies, district magnitude remains the single strongest institutional predictor of representation bias — ahead of malapportionment, the seat-allocation formula, or legal thresholds.



⚖️

Malapportionment isn’t systematically right-biased
Contrary to the anecdotal case of Spain, malapportionment shows no consistent ideological direction in lower chambers worldwide — it favours the left as often as the right. Upper chambers are the exception, leaning right.



🏛️

Reforms tend to democratize, not entrench
Historically, electoral reforms have leaned more towards democratization than towards protecting incumbents — governments in consolidated democracies show little systematic ability to gerrymander malapportionment to their own advantage.



🌍

A tool for — and against — minorities
Malapportionment has long been used to protect the representation of ethnic and national minorities, and remains widely used for that purpose in states transitioning between democracy and autocracy.



🚩

Autocrats reform when threatened
In authoritarian regimes, electoral reforms are activated above all when rulers perceive a threat to their power — and the more ethnically diverse the country, the more likely those reforms take a territorial form.



📱

Information reinforces, it rarely converts
A large-scale Voting Advice Application experiment in Spain shows personalized political information strengthens voters’ existing preferences, especially among the undecided — but does not trigger switching between parties.

title: Simulations
text:
Electoral institutions are difficult to study causally with observational data: they are jointly determined, endogenous, and rarely vary independently of one another. The REPBIAS simulation app addresses this by generating large numbers of synthetic polities in which four institutional parameters — malapportionment, district magnitude, the seat-allocation formula, and the legal electoral threshold — are introduced exogenously and independently of each other, decomposing total representation bias into the distinct share contributed by each one.
Use the controls inside the app below to set your own combination of institutions and see how the distortion — and its sources — change in real time.
